images.caption:
Gymnoderma lineare (A. Evans) Yoshim. & Sharp, 1968

(photograph of a herbarium specimen showing strap-shaped lobes)

Growing on acidic rock above 6,000 feet at Clingmans Dome, Sevier County, Tennessee, USA; collected and identified by Allen C. Skorepa (No. 6027, May 1967); specimen is now in the Lichen Herbarium of the New York Botanical Garden.

Gymnoderma lineare is a rare species that is on the U.S. Endangered Species List.

images.caption: Dead Fraser fir along the Clingmans Dome tower trail near the summit of Clingmans Dome in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee and North Carolina, in the southeastern United States.  The Fraser firs, which once dominated the higher parts of the Smokies, have largely been wiped out by the balsam wooly adelgid infestation.

The Fraser firs, which once dominated the higher parts of the Smokies, have largely been wiped out by the balsam wooly adelgid infestation.

images.caption: 180-degree stitched panoramic, looking north from the observation tower atop Clingmans Dome in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park of the southeastern United States.  Mount Buckley is the knob in the foreground on the lower left, with Thunderhead Mountain and Gregory Bald visible in the distance.  Pigeon Forge is at the top center, and Mount Le Conte is the large mountain right of center.  Mount Guyot is visible in the distance on the right.  Newfound Gap Road (US-441) is on the lower right.
images.alt: 180-degree stitched panoramic, looking north from the observation tower atop Clingmans Dome in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park of the southeastern United States.  Mount Buckley is the knob in the foreground on the lower left, with Thunderhead Mountain and Gregory Bald visible in the distance.  Pigeon Forge is at the top center, and Mount Le Conte is the large mountain right of center.  Mount Guyot is visible in the distance on the right.  Newfound Gap Road (US-441) is on the lower right.
